H1.why: The correlational claim -- stamp/occlusion documents show an elevated RATE of the undershoot defect -- is confirmed (29.31% vs 4.70%, an exact reproduction of 029's finding via an independent corpus-wide metric). But H1's specific MECHANISTIC claim, that stamp/occlusion causes MORE SEVERE bbox undershoot, is contradicted: among documents that do show the defect, stamp/occlusion magnitudes (1.10-1.47px) are smaller than non-stamp magnitudes (up to 15.40px). The stamp/occlusion sample is also only 4 distinct documents (58 arm-replications), too small to generalize with confidence. A clean, unconfounded natural experiment (hc_encoding_vi, no stamp/occlusion label, same document/route/milestone) shows the OCR recognizer alone determines whether the defect fires at all (0px under EasyOCR, 14.4-15.4px under four other recognizers) -- an equally strong, independently-demonstrated trigger H1 did not name.
H1.strongest_evidence: h1_resolution.json: h1_core_test (29.31% vs 4.70%, exact match to 029) and 2_2_component_attribution (0/1867 undershoot without synthesis, ruling out a synthesis-independent alternative)
H1.strongest_counterevidence: h1_resolution.json: critical_caveat_pseudo_replication.magnitude_finding (severity direction reversed vs prediction) and paired_comparisons.json pairing 1 (recognizer-driven firing on a non-stamp document, hc_encoding_vi)
H1.confidence_reasoning: high confidence in the measured facts (all numbers reproduced exactly against 029 and cross-verified); medium, not high, confidence in the CAUSAL interpretation because the stamp/occlusion sample is only 4 documents and pixel-level detector-confidence data (which would directly test the 'Table Transformer's own uncertainty' clause of H1) was not available to inspect this milestone
H1.what_would_change_verdict: pixel-level inspection of Table Transformer's confidence scores or attention on the 4 stamp-affected documents vs a matched sample of clean documents; or a larger stamp/occlusion sample from a corpus this repository does not currently have

H2.why: The exact discriminating test 029 specified -- do any of the 265 escaping cells intersect a table other than their own -- was run in full and found ZERO instances of contamination, an exact reproduction of the escaping-cell count (265) confirming the re-derivation is faithful. The evaluator used to test this was independently validated by a constructed adversarial case (H2-2) proving it WOULD detect contamination if present, so the null result is not an artifact of a broken checker. The corpus also contains a genuine (non-vacuous) precondition for contamination -- 25 same-page multi-table instances exist elsewhere in the corpus -- so the test was not trivially unfalsifiable, even though those specific instances never coincide with an escaping cell. The theoretical bound stated in H2 (escape cannot exceed roughly one token's own dimension, since admission requires center containment) held on every instance: max observed escape 14.43px, 0/265 exceeding a conservative 40px single-token proxy bound.
H2.strongest_evidence: h2_resolution.json: H2_CORE_RESULT (0/265 contaminated) and adversarial_controls.json H2-2 (evaluator proven capable of detecting contamination when deliberately constructed)
H2.strongest_counterevidence: h2_resolution.json: same_page_multi_table_precondition_check -- the specific co-occurrence of an escaping cell AND a neighboring table never arises in this corpus, so the geometric argument in H2's own statement (the true source of confidence) remains the primary evidence rather than this empirical test alone
H2.confidence_reasoning: the geometric bound in H2's own statement is a mathematical consequence of the center-containment admission rule (provenance.json claim 1-2), not merely an empirical observation -- a token's center inside table.bbox by construction bounds how far its edge can extend, by that same token's own dimension. This is as close to a proof as geometry allows, and the empirical test corroborates it without contradiction
H2.what_would_change_verdict: a corpus example with a stamp/occlusion table immediately adjacent (within one token-height) to a second table on the same page -- this repository does not currently contain one

priority_reassessment.029_original_recommendation: table-label gating under stamp/occlusion (025's Class D), not the row-synthesis mechanism, on grounds of higher severity (whole table lost) and a plausible shared root with the reading_order defect
priority_reassessment.does_it_change: NO -- same priority, but for a MODIFIED reason
priority_reassessment.reasoning: H2 SUPPORTED confirms the row-synthesis defect remains bounded and low-severity (no cross-table contamination, sub-15px magnitude) -- this REMOVES the one scenario (H2 falsified) that would have elevated it above table-label gating. H1 PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED weakens, rather than strengthens, the stamp/occlusion -> row-synthesis causal story specifically, but does NOT weaken 025's independent finding about table-label gating itself (025's finding is about the base.py:747 label-equality gate discarding a correctly-geometried region, a completely different code path from tier-3 synthesis, verified at the time to have a 100%-confirmed 3-document mechanism). The two defects remain what 029 found them to be: table-label gating is higher-severity (total table loss vs bounded pixel slop) and 030 adds no evidence either way on gating itself, since this milestone was scoped to H1/H2 only. One new consideration: H1's finding that OCR-recognizer choice, not stamp/occlusion, is the clearest demonstrated trigger for row-synthesis firing suggests that IF a fix to tier-3 synthesis is pursued (independently of the gating question), it should not be motivated by 'this mainly affects stamp/occlusion documents' -- that framing is now only partially supported.
priority_reassessment.verdict: SAME PRIORITY (table-label gating remains the higher-value target), reasoning partially revised
